ami_style_notes:
The meeting has a relaxed, collegial academic-video-call style, with mostly short to medium turns outside the formal presentations and long, structured monologues during talks. Early conversation is highly overlapping and fragmented, with frequent greetings, side comments, technical-check questions, and several people chiming in with brief affirmations like “yeah,” “okay,” or laughter-like reactions. Speakers use abundant fillers and repairs—“um,” “uh,” repeated words, false starts, self-corrections, and unfinished phrasing—especially in spontaneous discussion, while maintaining a generally warm, informal tone. Introductions and presentations shift to a more formal, appreciative register, though presenters still hedge heavily with phrases such as “I think,” “sort of,” “maybe,” “likely,” and “we’re interested in.” Questions are often prefaced with praise, disclaimers (“quick question,” “naive question”), and lengthy setup before the actual question. Participants challenge or extend points indirectly and constructively, usually framing alternatives as curiosities or open questions rather than disagreement; answers acknowledge uncertainty, qualify claims, and invite future collaboration.

Meeting style for this meeting (one_voice_leads): One person (often the most senior) talks for much of the meeting in long turns. Others come in with short questions or one-line agreement. A quieter person speaks rarely and usually only when asked directly or after a pause.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - So what I keep coming back to, and this is just from the last couple of projects I've run, is that you pay for it later if you skip the pilot, you always do, and then...
  - Mm.
  - Sorry, can I ask- is that the same pilot as the spring one?
Opening: Start with a person asking for a quick catch-up because they missed the last meeting.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Evaluating a program in which community health workers visit patients with uncontrolled high blood pressure at home.

speakers.name: Dr. Elena Park
speakers.background: Dr. Park is a general internist and cardiovascular outcomes postdoctoral researcher with 6 years of clinical practice and 4 years evaluating hypertension quality-improvement initiatives in safety-net primary care. She works with electronic health record extracts, chart review, and pragmatic comparative designs, and has collaborated with clinic teams on blood-pressure measurement protocols and medication-management workflows.
speakers.distinct_perspective: She frames the program primarily as a clinically actionable pathway from uncontrolled blood pressure to follow-up care. She prioritizes a clear, interpretable blood-pressure endpoint, clinically recognizable eligibility criteria, and a design that can be implemented without disrupting clinics. She is attentive to whether recorded measurements and medication changes are meaningful in routine care, while relying on colleagues to judge implementation equity and social-process questions.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

speakers.name: Dr. Malik Okafor
speakers.background: Dr. Okafor is a medical sociologist with 14 years of experience studying trust, institutional navigation, and racialized disparities in urban health-care systems. His research combines semi-structured interviews, ethnographic fieldwork, workflow observation, and thematic analysis, often focusing on how frontline workers translate institutional expectations into relationships with patients. He has led several mixed-methods evaluations involving community health workers and federally qualified health centers.
speakers.distinct_perspective: He treats CHW visits as relational labor embedded in unequal institutional conditions rather than as a uniform dose of service. He is interested in how trust, credibility, stigma, language, and patients' prior encounters with care shape engagement. He favors qualitative accounts that can identify mechanisms and meanings, but will work within operational constraints when the team needs a feasible, bounded study.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

speakers.name: Priya Shah
speakers.background: Priya Shah is a public health evaluation specialist with 11 years of experience in municipal health departments and community-based chronic-disease programs. She has designed performance dashboards, equity stratifications, referral-flow monitoring systems, and implementation budgets for programs serving linguistically diverse and underinsured populations. Her usual methods include descriptive surveillance, process indicators, denominator construction, and rapid-cycle reporting using routinely collected administrative and EHR data.
speakers.distinct_perspective: She views the evaluation as a public accountability and implementation-management tool: it must show who was reached, where people were lost along the referral pathway, whether access differs across population groups, and whether the program can operate within available capacity. She pushes for measures that are reportable on schedule and usable by clinic and health-department leaders, while recognizing that causal evaluation design and clinical measurement choices require input from the other leads.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: uncertain about how their methods apply to this problem

meeting_opening: Start with a person asking for a quick catch-up because they missed the last meeting.
benchmark_task: Give a meeting where researchers finalize decisions relying on both explicit and implicit assumptions. The evaluated AI must identify the decision-relevant assumptions. Provide a proposed reference answer with evidence; implicit assumptions should be inferable, not invented.

seed_spec.benchmark_task: Give a meeting where researchers finalize decisions relying on both explicit and implicit assumptions. The evaluated AI must identify the decision-relevant assumptions. Provide a proposed reference answer with evidence; implicit assumptions should be inferable, not invented.
seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Hold a planning meeting in which the three leads finalize an evaluation design, eligibility definition, primary outcome, data sources, equity reporting approach, and a streamlined qualitative component. Ensure the following information emerges naturally. Dr. Park proposes a stepped-wedge rollout across the three clinics, with one clinic beginning the intensified referral workflow every four months, and states that the primary outcome will be change in systolic blood pressure at six months using the most recent clinic-recorded measurement. She says the clinics' usual care will remain stable enough for staggered timing to provide a comparison and that medication changes will be recorded in the electronic health record. Priya Shah agrees to use referral, completed-visit, and six-month blood-pressure data to create a reach-and-equity dashboard by clinic, race/ethnicity, preferred language, insurance status, and neighborhood deprivation. She states that missing demographic fields and absent follow-up blood-pressure readings can be treated as exclusions from the relevant dashboard calculations because the health department needs a simple report by the deadline. She also decides the existing 180-referral annual capacity is sufficient for the proposed rollout and that no additional outreach budget is needed. Dr. Okafor agrees to conduct interviews with 12 CHWs and 18 patients who completed at least two home visits, rather than observing visits or interviewing people who declined referral or did not complete visits. He explains that this will efficiently document how trust is built during the intervention. The group agrees not to collect home blood-pressure readings as outcome data because they consider clinic readings more standardized. They approve the plan without adding a fidelity assessment beyond CHW visit-completion logs. Do not have participants label these as assumptions or debate the benchmark task. Include ordinary operational reasoning and final decisions, while leaving the listed decisions in place.

transcript.speaker: Priya Shah
transcript.text: Hi, everyone—sorry, I missed the tail end of the last meeting, so could I get a really quick catch-up on where we landed? For today, I'm hoping we can get clear enough on the routine data and the actual workflow to lock a usable 12-month dashboard and the implementation budget before 15 May, and then...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Park
transcript.text: We were leaning toward a stepped rollout of the intensified referral workflow, with one clinic every four months, and keeping the usual pathway otherwise unchanged. Clinically, I'd keep eligibility at two recent readings of at least 140/90. The main outcome would be the six-month change in the latest clinic-recorded systolic pressure, though I still need to confirm the extract can reliably capture that and medication changes.

transcript.speaker: Priya Shah
transcript.text: That works for the dashboard if the clinic systolic field is genuinely comparable. Elena, have you seen enough similarity in BP documentation across the three sites that we can treat that latest clinic-recorded value as one measure? And I’d want the rollout extract to retain the referral date, visit completion, and a six-month BP-record flag. Otherwise, we won’t know whether a null outcome is loss to follow-up or no measurement.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Park
transcript.text: I've only done a small pull, so I wouldn't say that yet. The fields look broadly similar, but I need to check how often each site records a repeat versus, um, just taking the initial automated value, and whether the extract preserves that. I agree on the BP-record flag. Otherwise a missing six-month value is doing too much work.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Malik Okafor
transcript.text: Mm, that missingness matters.

transcript.speaker: Priya Shah
transcript.text: For the leadership report, I’d separate that out right away. Denominator eligible, referred, reached for a first visit, completed visits, and then had a clinic BP documented by six months. Malik, on the referral side, have you heard from participants what makes that first contact feel, um, credible rather than like another burden?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Malik Okafor
transcript.text: What I’ve heard in the preliminary conversations is that credibility is pretty practical. The CHW follows through on a pharmacy call, explains a letter, helps get a ride. Those are small things that distinguish them from another institutional outreach. I’d be cautious about reducing that to a contact count, though, because whether that first contact lands as supportive or burdensome is very, very contingent on prior care experiences.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Park
transcript.text: Yeah, that makes sense.

transcript.speaker: Priya Shah
transcript.text: And I think we can preserve that without pretending it's fidelity scoring. Could the existing completion log carry a very light, structured reason for contact or referral support, pharmacy, transport, appointment navigation, that sort of thing, or is even that outside what CHWs already document? For the dashboard, the pathway counts still matter, but they shouldn't imply every, every completed visit was equivalent.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Malik Okafor
transcript.text: I think a light field could be useful if it stays descriptive, rather than making the CHWs code their relational work on the spot. Maybe broad categories plus an "other practical support" option, because explaining a benefits letter or doing a pharmacy call can be the thing that makes the next visit possible, and it won't always fit neatly. I'd want to see the current log first, though. I don't want to add documentation that, um, takes away from the visit.

transcript.speaker: Priya Shah
transcript.text: Let’s look at the current log before we add anything. With the 180-referral annual capacity, I really don’t think we should create a parallel outreach or documentation layer. Broad support categories only if they fit what’s already there. Otherwise, the referral-to-first-visit and completion measures are the cleanest operational signal, but...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Malik Okafor
transcript.text: I’d keep the qualitative piece deliberately bounded. We could do interviews with 12 CHWs and 18 patients who complete at least two visits. That gets at what those broad categories- how practical help becomes credible, what they miss, without asking the clinics or the CHWs to carry a separate data-collection burden.

transcript.speaker: Priya Shah
transcript.text: That seems proportionate, especially if we’re not asking clinics to staff it. With capacity at about 180 referrals a year, I’d keep the dashboard’s core reach denominator as all eligible patients, and then show referral uptake separately. Otherwise the interviews of people with two visits will be really useful context, but they’ll necessarily miss where the pathway first breaks.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Malik Okafor
transcript.text: The interviews won’t tell us much about the people who never get reached, and I don’t think we should make them pretend to. If the dashboard can show where that attrition sits, then the interview sample can be much more modestly about the mechanisms of engagement once a relationship has actually, actually begun.

transcript.speaker: Priya Shah
transcript.text: With only about 180 referrals over the year, the operational denominators should be manageable clinic by clinic. Eligible, referred, first visit, completed visits, then six-month BP on record. I’d stratify those by the usual equity fields, though I need to check whether we can actually link neighborhood deprivation, um, from the address data in the routine extract.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Malik Okafor
transcript.text: Mm. I’d be interested in whether the address fields are stable enough for that linkage, especially for people moving between clinics or in temporary housing. Otherwise deprivation can become another selectively missing variable. And Priya, do your dashboards show whether a completed visit gets recorded consistently when people cross clinic sites or contact the CHW through different, um, routes?

transcript.speaker: Priya Shah
transcript.text: Not reliably, no. I'd need to inspect the referral and CHW log identifiers before I promise that. We can probably distinguish the originating clinic from the clinic where the follow-up BP was recorded, but cross-site contact could muddy a clinic-specific completion rate. With only 180 referrals a year, I'd rather resolve that in the extract than patch it with a new workflow.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Park
transcript.text: And for the clinical extract, I'd want the originating clinic and the site of the follow-up reading kept separate. Someone can still meet eligibility, eligibility with two recent clinic pressures at or above 140/90, and then get follow-up somewhere else. I wouldn't want that to look like the intervention failed just because the BP was recorded across sites.

transcript.speaker: Priya Shah
transcript.text: Separating originating clinic from follow-up site is the right way to do it. For the operational dashboard, I’d attribute referral and CHW completion to the originating clinic, then report six-month BP documentation regardless of where it was captured, with the follow-up site retained as a field. At roughly 180 referrals a year, that should still be, be quite tractable.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Park
transcript.text: And the eligibility rule should stay fixed. It needs to be two recent clinic readings of at least 140/90 mmHg across all three sites.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Malik Okafor
transcript.text: And Elena, on the medication-change field, when we see one in the EHR, what can we actually infer? Is that usually evidence of a clinical encounter and treatment adjustment, or could it just as easily be a refill or somebody cleaning up the med list? I’d be wary of narrating it as engagement with care without, without knowing that.

transcript.speaker: Priya Shah
transcript.text: Hm, that’s an important distinction.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Park
transcript.text: In this setting, a medication-change field is pretty noisy. It can be a real start, stop, or dose change after a visit, but it can also be reconciliation or a refill artifact, so I’d treat it as a secondary descriptive measure unless the extract lets us distinguish prescription orders from list cleanup. And the small chart pull is actually- that’s why I don’t want to infer too much from it.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Malik Okafor
transcript.text: Right, that’s pretty noisy.

transcript.speaker: Priya Shah
transcript.text: Then I’d leave medication change out of the core performance display entirely. Maybe retain it in the analytic file as a qualified secondary field. For the May 15 plan, keep the core very lean, the pathway through six-month BP documentation, with the 180-referral annual capacity as the planning assumption.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Malik Okafor
transcript.text: Okay, I think we've got what we needed for today. Let's pick this back up once the extract checks are in. Thanks, both.

transcript.speaker: Priya Shah
transcript.text: Sounds good—take care, both.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Park
transcript.text: Thanks, bye.

realism_signals: uneven turn lengths, including short reactions and backchannels
imperfect coherence: tangents, small misunderstandings, points that get dropped or repeated
issues: Core seed and ground-truth conditions are missing or contradicted: no speaker states that usual care and other clinic conditions will remain stable enough for staggered timing to serve as a comparison. Turn 2 proposes staggered rollout, but the explicit stepped-wedge validity assumption is absent.

The transcript never states or decides that home blood-pressure readings will not be collected because clinic readings are more standardized. Instead, turns 3-4 explicitly leave comparability of clinic measurements unresolved, so the primary-outcome assumption is not cleanly supported.

Priya does not create the required equity dashboard stratified by race/ethnicity, preferred language, insurance status, and neighborhood deprivation. Turn 15 mentions only unspecified “usual equity fields” and possible deprivation linkage; race/ethnicity, language, and insurance are never identified.

The required explicit decision to exclude missing demographic fields and absent six-month BP readings from relevant dashboard calculations is absent and effectively contradicted. Turns 3-4 and 6 treat missing BP as something to flag and report rather than exclude, while demographic missingness is not addressed.

The qualitative component is materially changed: turn 12 samples patients completing at least two visits, not two home visits; it does not explicitly rule out observation, decliners, or non-completers.
